faq.a: Yes, amyopathic DM presents with skin findings alone; monitor for later muscle involvement.
faq.q: Can dermatomyositis occur without muscle weakness?

faq.a: Steroid toxicity (infection, diabetes, osteoporosis) is high; add a steroid‑sparing agent early.
faq.q: Why avoid long‑term high‑dose steroids alone?

faq.a: Not if clinical, CK, and antibody data are convincing; biopsy is reserved for atypical cases.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with heliotrope rash and proximal weakness – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order CK and myositis‑specific antibodies; if positive, start steroids while arranging biopsy.
How does DM differ from PM on muscle biopsy? — DM shows perifascicular atrophy and complement deposition; PM shows endomysial CD8+ T‑cell infiltrates.

A patient with HIV on ART presents with proximal weakness and CK 3× ULN – how do you distinguish HIV‑myopathy from IIM? — Review CD4 count, ART timing, and skin findings; IIM often has rash and higher CK.

Why is methotrexate preferred over cyclophosphamide as a steroid‑sparing agent in most cases? — Methotrexate has a better safety profile and is effective for chronic disease; cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ involvement.
What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral in DM? — Rapidly progressive dysphagia or dyspnoea indicating airway or respiratory muscle compromise.
Explain the rationale for malignancy screening in adult DM patients. — Up to 20% have an associated cancer; early detection improves outcomes, especially for ovarian, lung, and colorectal cancers.
A patient cannot afford MRI; how would you still stage disease severity? — Use CK level, manual muscle testing (MRC), and functional questionnaires (HAQ‑D).
What is the significance of anti‑Mi‑2 antibodies? — Strongly associated with classic DM skin findings and a relatively good prognosis.
ai.title: Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inflammatory myopathies causing proximal muscle weakness and skin rash (dermatomyositis). Autoimmune, but infections and drugs are common triggers in low‑resource settings. Early recognition prevents irreversible weakness and life‑threatening complications.

b: DM: muscle weakness + heliotrope rash, Gottron papules
sections.p: Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are systemic autoimmune diseases that target skeletal muscle. DM adds characteristic skin findings. Both present with symmetric proximal weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy.

b: EULAR/ACR score uses age, skin involvement, CK, EMG, biopsy, and auto‑antibodies
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on the 2017 EULAR/ACR classification criteria (score ≥7 for definite IIM). Severity is staged by muscle strength (MRC scale) and functional impact (HAQ‑D).

b: Screen for hepatitis B before immunosuppression
Look for interstitial lung disease with dyspnoea
sections.p: In East Africa, HIV, hepatitis B, and malaria can mimic or trigger IIM. Untreated disease may lead to respiratory failure, dysphagia, cardiac involvement, or malignancy (especially in DM).
When MRI or EMG are unavailable, rely on CK, ANA, and clinical pattern; a trial of steroids can be diagnostic.

t.b: Is there muscle injury? – CK > 5× upper limit supports IIM

t.a: ANA and myositis‑specific antibodies (Mi‑2, Jo‑1, MDA5)
t.b: Which subtype or associated malignancy? – Positive Jo‑1 suggests antisynthetase syndrome
Is the pattern inflammatory? – Short, polyphasic motor units with fibrillation potentials
Where is active inflammation? – Hyperintense T2 signal in proximal muscles
What is the histology? – Endomysial CD8+ infiltrates (PM) or perifascicular atrophy with complement deposition (DM)
Is there interstitial lung disease? – Ground‑glass opacities suggest pulmonary involvement

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, ESR, CRP, liver function)
t.b: Are there systemic inflammation or drug‑related toxicity? – Elevated ESR/CRP common

b: Methotrexate or azathioprine – steroid‑sparing, monitor liver and blood counts
IVIG – reserved for refractory disease or when infection risk limits steroids
Physiotherapy – prevents contractures and improves strength
Screen for malignancy in DM (age‑appropriate ultrasound/clinical exam) – early detection improves survival
sections.p: First‑line therapy is high‑dose oral prednisone (or IV methylprednisolone if severe). Add steroid‑sparing agents early to limit toxicity.

b: HIV‑associated myopathy – usually CK modestly raised, improves with ART
Statin‑induced myopathy – drug history, CK often <10× ULN, stops when drug stopped
Systemic lupus erythematosus – rash is malar, not Gottron papules; ANA pattern differs
sections.p: Conditions that cause proximal weakness or rash can be mistaken for IIM.

b: Normal CK does not exclude DM if skin signs are present
EMG false‑negative if performed after steroids started
sections.p: CK may be normal in chronic disease; EMG can be normal early; skin rash may be subtle in dark‑skinned patients.

b: Ask about recent infections, herbal remedies, and HIV status
Examine for heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and mechanic’s hands
Test for dysphagia – early referral for speech therapy
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, trigger identification, and safe immunosuppression.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening dyspnoea (possible ILD or respiratory failure)
New cardiac arrhythmia or heart failure signs
